title: N.I.C.E. Design Process
text:
By the end of this page:

I will be able to move from a real situation to a testable idea.
I will be able to use evidence and feedback to decide what to change.

This is important because a good project solves a real need and improves through testing.
Start with the situation, move through N.I.C.E., and repeat the process after evaluation. Each step produces something useful for the next step.

title: N.I.C.E. Design Process
text:
By the end of this page:

I will be able to move from a real situation to a testable idea.
I will be able to use evidence and feedback to decide what to change.

This is important because a good project solves a real need and improves through testing.
Start with the situation, move through N.I.C.E., and repeat the process after evaluation. Each step produces something useful for the next step.

title: N.I.C.E. Design Process
text:
Situation: understand what is happening



Separate what is known from what still needs to be checked. Figure from the class slide deck.


Before choosing a solution, describe the real situation.

Facts can be observed or supported with evidence.
Assumptions may be true, but still need to be checked.
Interpretations are what you think the facts mean. They can change when you learn more.

The result is a clear situation statement that does not jump ahead to a product or solution.
Use the N.I.C.E. Needs Worksheet to record the situation, users, facts, assumptions, questions, and restrictions.

title: N.I.C.E. Design Process
text:
N: Needs and Necessities



Define what the solution must accomplish before deciding what to make. Figure from the class slide deck.


Turn the situation into requirements.

A need describes what the solution should accomplish.
A necessity is a requirement that must be met.
A nice-to-have would improve the solution but is not essential.
Priorities show which requirements matter most.

The result is a clear need statement and a prioritized list of requirements. Describe the function you need, not a product you have already decided to build.
Continue in the N.I.C.E. Needs Worksheet to write the need statement and rank the necessities and nice-to-haves.

title: N.I.C.E. Design Process
text:
I: Investigate and Inquire



Research begins with questions and comparison, not a random search. Figure from the class slide deck.


Find out what already exists and what the evidence suggests.

What do we need?
What solutions already exist?
What could work for this situation?
What should be improved, combined, simplified, or changed?

Compare each idea with the needs, necessities, and priorities. The result is an evidence-based direction and a reason for choosing it.
Use the N.I.C.E. Inquiry Worksheet to ask questions, compare existing solutions, and decide what to adapt.

title: N.I.C.E. Design Process
text:
C: Create and Communicate



Make the idea visible, explain it clearly, and ask for useful feedback. Figure from the class slide deck.


Create a sketch, model, prototype, or other representation that lets someone understand the idea. Explain the situation, the need, and how the idea helps. Then ask specific questions instead of only asking, “Do you like it?”
A short pitch can follow this sequence:

Have you ever experienced this situation?
Have you needed or wanted this improvement?
Our idea is… It helps by…

The result is a clear pitch, useful feedback, and one specific change to consider.
Use the communication worksheets in order:

Communicate Worksheet Online or Pitch and Show Your Idea Print to explain and show the idea.
Feedback Package to collect specific feedback and find patterns.
Plan and Plan Feedback to identify resources, roles, steps, and improvements to the plan.

title: N.I.C.E. Design Process
text:
E: Evaluate



Use evidence to decide what to keep, change, remove, or test next. Figure from the class slide deck.


Compare the idea or prototype with the original situation and the prioritized requirements. Check whether earlier assumptions were correct. Look for patterns in testing and feedback rather than reacting to one random comment.
Decide what to keep, change, remove, or test next. The result is a revised solution supported by evidence and reasons.
Use the N.I.C.E. Evaluate Worksheet to connect the feedback to a justified next change.

title: N.I.C.E. Design Process
text:
Repeat the cycle



Evaluation leads to the next version, not simply the end of the project. Figure from the class slide deck.


Return to the needs after evaluation. Ask what the evidence proved, which assumption was wrong, which requirement matters most now, and what the next version should change. Design improves through these repeated, evidence-based decisions.
Use the N.I.C.E. Design Log to keep the worksheets, sketches, feedback, decisions, and later versions together.

title: N.I.C.E. Design Process
text:
Watch and use

Engineering design process review: notice how the process moves from a problem to testing.
Pitch the idea: notice the sequence problem, idea, show it, ask.
Open the complete N.I.C.E. slide deck.
Open all N.I.C.E. worksheets, completed examples, and classroom materials.

title: Lesson 1: Build the Nameplate Text in Photopea
text:
By the end of this lesson:

I can make an 11 × 4 inch canvas.
I can leave a 4 × 4 inch space for a logo.
I can try fonts and choose one that is easy to read.
I can save a PSD and export a transparent PNG and SVG.

title: Lesson 1: Build the Nameplate Text in Photopea
text:
By the end of this lesson:

I can make an 11 × 4 inch canvas.
I can leave a 4 × 4 inch space for a logo.
I can try fonts and choose one that is easy to read.
I can save a PSD and export a transparent PNG and SVG.

title: Lesson 1: Build the Nameplate Text in Photopea
text:
Why this is useful
A clear nameplate is easier to read and easier to change. The empty space on the left gives the logo a planned place instead of squeezing it in later.
You will use this file again in Lesson 3.

title: Lesson 1: Build the Nameplate Text in Photopea
text:
What you will make
You will make a transparent 11 × 4 inch nameplate. The left 4 × 4 inches stay empty. The name Andrade sits in the right part of the design.


Your browser cannot play this video. Use the screenshots and steps below.

title: Lesson 1: Build the Nameplate Text in Photopea
text:
Before you start
Open Photopea in a browser.
You will use:

the Type Tool (T);
a vertical guide;
the Move Tool (V); and
the Layers panel.

title: Lesson 1: Build the Nameplate Text in Photopea
text:
1. Make the canvas

Choose File > New.
Set Width to 11 inches.
Set Height to 4 inches.
Set DPI to 300.
Set Background to Transparent.
Choose Create.

Photopea will make a 3300 × 1200 pixel canvas. That is correct for 11 × 4 inches at 300 pixels per inch.



Photopea’s New Project window set to 11 inches wide, 4 inches high, and 300 pixels per inch.

title: Lesson 1: Build the Nameplate Text in Photopea
text:
2. Mark the logo space
The logo space is a 4 × 4 inch square on the left.

Choose View > New Guide.
Choose a Vertical guide.
Enter 4 in. If Photopea asks for pixels, enter 1200 px.
Choose OK.

Everything left of the guide is for the logo. Keep the name to the right of it.



A vertical guide marks four inches from the left side of the transparent nameplate.

title: Lesson 1: Build the Nameplate Text in Photopea
text:
3. Type the name

Select the Type Tool (T).
Click to the right of the guide.
Type Andrade.
Select the whole word before changing the font.




The name Andrade added to the right side of the nameplate.

title: Lesson 1: Build the Nameplate Text in Photopea
text:
4. Try several fonts
Try at least three fonts. Change only the font at first. This makes the choices easier to compare.
Try:

a serif font;
a decorative or rounded font; and
a plain sans serif font.

A serif font has small finishing strokes on the letters. A sans serif font does not. Sans serif letters often stay clear when they are engraved or read from far away.



Andrade shown in a serif font while the student compares font choices.


Ask these questions:

Can I read the name quickly?
Are any letters too thin?
Does the name feel calm and balanced?
Will the letters still be clear when the nameplate is made?

The example ends with DejaVu Sans Book at about 300 px. Another clear sans serif font is also fine.

title: Lesson 1: Build the Nameplate Text in Photopea
text:
5. Place the name

Select the Move Tool (V).
Keep the name inside the right 7 inches.
Centre it from top to bottom.
Leave a clear margin on the right.
Check that the name does not cross the 4 inch guide.

Use your eyes as well as the numbers. The empty space above and below the name should look even.



Andrade in a balanced sans serif font with room for a logo on the left.



Check your work
Continue when:

the canvas is 11 × 4 inches;
the background is transparent;
the left 4 × 4 inch area is empty;
the name is easy to read;
the name is centred from top to bottom; and
there is a good margin on the right.

title: Lesson 1: Build the Nameplate Text in Photopea
text:
6. Save and export
Save three files.

Choose File > Save as PSD. Name it Andrade-nameplate-text.psd.
Choose File > Export as > PNG. Name it Andrade-nameplate-text.png.
Choose File > Export as > SVG. Name it Andrade-nameplate-text.svg.

Keep add raster graphics off when you export the SVG. The checkerboard means the background is transparent. It will not appear in the saved image.



Photopea’s Export as menu with PNG and SVG choices visible.



Download the example files

Editable PSD
Transparent PNG
Vector SVG

title: Lesson 1: Build the Nameplate Text in Photopea
text:
Common issues

The canvas has a white box: make a new file with Background: Transparent.
The name is in the logo space: move it to the right of the 4 inch guide.
The name looks too small: make the type larger, but keep a clear right margin.
The name is hard to read: choose a simple sans serif font with open letter shapes.
The name moved when the font changed: use the Move Tool to centre it again.


Design curriculum: Complete this lesson after the N.I.C.E. Design Process. Next, use a rough sketch to make a clean logo in Lesson 2. You will combine both files in Lesson 3.

title: Lesson 1: Build the Nameplate Text in Photopea
text:
Summary
You made an 11 × 4 inch transparent nameplate. You left a 4 × 4 inch space for a logo, tried several fonts, chose a balanced sans serif font, and saved PSD, PNG, and SVG files.
Next: Lesson 2: Trace a Rough Logo in Photopea.

title: Lesson 2: Trace a Rough Logo in Photopea
text:
By the end of this activity:

I can open a sketch in Photopea.
I can trace the sketch with editable lines.
I can make both sides of a logo look even.
I can save a PSD and export an SVG.

title: Lesson 2: Trace a Rough Logo in Photopea
text:
By the end of this activity:

I can open a sketch in Photopea.
I can trace the sketch with editable lines.
I can make both sides of a logo look even.
I can save a PSD and export an SVG.

title: Lesson 2: Trace a Rough Logo in Photopea
text:
Why this is useful
Your first sketch does not need to be perfect. Editable lines let you fix the shape while keeping the original idea.
You can use this skill for logos, signs, stickers, name tags, and laser projects. The PSD keeps your work editable. The SVG stays sharp when it is made larger or smaller.

title: Lesson 2: Trace a Rough Logo in Photopea
text:
What you are making
You will start with a photo of a hand-drawn mark. You will rebuild it with four clean lines. The sketch gives you the idea. You decide the final shape.
The example uses four vector strokes:

a left diagonal;
a right diagonal;
a vertical centre line; and
a horizontal crossbar.







TipWork from large shapes to small corrections



Build the complete symbol first. Hide the photograph only after all four strokes exist, then judge the clean silhouette and make corrections.

title: Lesson 2: Trace a Rough Logo in Photopea
text:
Before you start
Open Photopea in a modern browser. You can choose File > Open or drag the photograph from its folder onto Photopea.
Complete Lesson 1: Build the Nameplate Text first. You will add this logo to that nameplate in Lesson 3.
You will use these parts of the editor:

Toolbar: the vertical row of tools on the left.
Canvas: the document in the centre.
Layers panel: the list of editable pieces on the right.
Shape layer: an editable line or shape that stays sharp when you resize it.
Stroke width: the thickness of a line.

title: Lesson 2: Trace a Rough Logo in Photopea
text:
1. Open the sketch
Open the photograph and fit it on screen. Do not erase or paint on it. It is only a reference for the vector shapes you will place above it.



A blue hand-drawn AA logo opened as a reference image in Photopea.


Look for the simple shapes inside the drawing. In this example, check the top point, the two sloped legs, the centre line, and the crossbar.

title: Lesson 2: Trace a Rough Logo in Photopea
text:
2. Draw the first editable stroke

Select the Line tool. If it is hidden, press and hold the shape-tool icon in the toolbar and choose Line.
In the top options bar, choose Shape mode.
Choose black for the line and begin with a stroke width near 14 px.
Drag from one endpoint to the other to trace the left diagonal.




The first black vector line drawn over one side of the blue sketch.


Photopea makes a new shape layer. A brush line is made of pixels. A shape line stays editable and sharp.






NoteThe sketch is a guide, not a rule



Aim for a cleaner angle than the hand-drawn line. Ignore small bumps and changes in pen pressure.

title: Lesson 2: Trace a Rough Logo in Photopea
text:
3. Build the complete symbol
Draw the remaining diagonal, the vertical centre stroke, and the crossbar. Keep each stroke as an editable shape layer.



Four black vector strokes forming the AA logo over the original sketch, with separate shape layers visible.


Work slowly and check these parts:

The two diagonal legs meet at one centred top point.
The lower endpoints of the legs are at the same height.
The vertical stroke is straight and centred.
The crossbar is level.
All four lines have a similar thickness.

It is fine if the first version is uneven. The next step is where the design work happens.

title: Lesson 2: Trace a Rough Logo in Photopea
section: 4. Hide the photo and check the logo
text:
4. Hide the photo and check the logo
In the Layers panel, click the eye beside the photograph layer. The grey-and-white checkerboard means the background is transparent.



The traced AA logo by itself on Photopea’s transparent checkerboard.


The clean logo is easier to check when the photo is hidden. Ask:

Does the logo lean to one side?
Are the two legs equally far from the centre?
Is the centre stroke truly vertical?
Is the crossbar centred and level?
Does one line look thicker than the others?

title: Lesson 2: Trace a Rough Logo in Photopea
section: 5. Fix the size, spacing, and line thickness
text:
5. Fix the size, spacing, and line thickness
Select one shape layer at a time. Use the Move tool to reposition a whole stroke or the Direct Select tool to adjust its vector points. Change the stroke width in the top options bar when a line looks too heavy or too light.
Make one small change at a time. Then look at the whole logo again. The two sides should look even.



A corrected, balanced black AA logo on a transparent background in Photopea.



Check your work
Continue only when:

the top point is centred;
the two outside legs feel balanced;
the centre stroke is straight;
the crossbar is level and centred; and
the line thickness looks the same.

title: Lesson 2: Trace a Rough Logo in Photopea
text:
6. Save the editable working file
Choose File > Save as PSD and use a clear filename such as initials-logo-working.psd.
The PSD is the working file. It preserves the photograph and the editable shape layers, so you can revise the logo later.

title: Lesson 2: Trace a Rough Logo in Photopea
text:
7. Export the SVG

Hide the photograph and any abandoned practice layers.
Choose File > Export as > SVG.
Leave add hidden layers off.
Leave add raster graphics off so the photograph is not embedded.
Keep the original width and height, then choose Save.




Photopea’s Save for Web window with SVG selected as the export format.


The downloaded .svg is the final artwork. It can be large on a sign or small on a label without becoming blurry.



The completed AA logo in Photopea with a notification confirming the SVG download.

title: Lesson 2: Trace a Rough Logo in Photopea
text:
Submit
Submit both files:

the .psd working file with editable shape layers; and
the final .svg with only the finished vector artwork visible.

title: Lesson 2: Trace a Rough Logo in Photopea
text:
Common issues

A line is on the photograph layer: undo, choose the Line tool in Shape mode, and draw it again.
A line is too thick or thin: select its shape layer and change the stroke width in the top options bar.
The logo looks good over the sketch but wrong alone: keep the photo hidden while you fix the size and spacing.
The photo appears in the SVG: hide the photo and export again with add hidden layers and add raster graphics turned off.


Design curriculum: This is Lesson 2 in the Photopea sequence. Complete Lesson 1 first. Next, add the finished logo to the nameplate in Lesson 3.

title: Lesson 2: Trace a Rough Logo in Photopea
text:
Summary
You used a rough sketch as a guide. You traced it with editable lines. You hid the photo, made both sides look even, saved a PSD, and exported an SVG.
Do not copy every wobble in the sketch. Keep the idea, use simple lines, and make the spacing and thickness look even.
Previous: Lesson 1: Build the Nameplate Text. Next: Lesson 3: Combine the Logo and Nameplate.

title: Laser Cutting for Technology Education | SVG, Kerf, Fits & Fabrication
text:
These canonical notes support a simple first TAS project and a deeper reusable fabrication pathway. Students can learn engraving versus cutting, SVG preparation, scale, material measurement, kerf, fit, holes, slots/tabs, supports, assemblies, hybrid fabrication and testing without treating every lesson as a required project.
The learning sequence lives here. The separate Laser Fabrication Library holds downloadable SVGs, calibration files, editable geometry, project components, holders, and inspiration.
For the active name-tag project, use the classroom toolkit. For advanced work, the toolkit also includes component palettes, standing-name-tag ideas, five pill-bottle organizer references and teaching slides. For repeated holes and measured plates, open the Fabrication Plate Builder, then verify the result with the material-fit calibration workflow.
For a freestanding holder, use the Laser-Cut Leg & Support Builder to generate measured legs, matching slots and a fit coupon, then read Make It Stand to check the load path and stability.

title: Laser Cutting for Technology Education | SVG, Kerf, Fits & Fabrication
text:

First, students use the three Photopea walkthroughs to follow the worked ANDRADE example. Next, they design their own name + logo name tag, compare fonts and layouts, and get teacher approval. Then they use the approved files to prepare the machine job, engrave the name tag, and evaluate spacing and legibility.

Possible contexts

Machine shop: drill bits, end mills, collets, precision drivers, or measuring tools.

Woodshop: chisels, files, drill bits, sanding tools, or layout tools.

title: Tool Organizer | General Fabrication Project / Advanced Extension
text:
Design criteria
Measure the actual tools and account for tapers, collars, handles, cords, and the hand position used during removal. Organize repeated geometry deliberately. Provide labels or silhouettes where they improve return-to-home behaviour. Test one-hand removal, visibility, reach, clearance, and whether neighbouring tools collide.
Browse the purpose-built holder kits for construction ideas. They are unverified starting geometry, not substitutes for measuring the class tools or testing the assembly.
Before an independent holder, study the Tool Organizer Gallery. Compare the interfaces, load path, assembly order, and physical-test status. Students should be able to explain which pattern transfers to their chosen tool family and which dimensions do not.
See actual build evidence and the knife-holder design review in the Tool Organizer Gallery.
For the concise classroom assignment, use the Tool Organizer Project. Students compare existing products and builds, then create an original holder and document prototype tests and revisions.

title: Tool Organizer | General Fabrication Project / Advanced Extension
text:
Required evidence
Include attributed precedents, a tool-measurement table, alternatives, selected concept, critical-dimension prototype, user test, revision notes, and a final evaluation against the identified need.

Ontario curriculum relevance: Particularly useful for TIJ1O, TMJ2O, TTJ2O, and TCJ2O. Electronics holders can support TEJ2O and senior computer-engineering contexts. Course relevance depends on the actual tools, users, and fabrication process selected.

title: Laser-Cut Leg & Support Builder
section: Choose the support by the force path
text:
Choose the support by the force path

Straight tabbed pair: locates two members in the front plane. It still needs a separate base that provides front-to-back depth.
Angled tabbed pair: spreads the feet sideways in the front view. It still needs a separate base or rear support for front-to-back stability.
Triangular side cheeks: can carry a plaque between two side panels, but this generator does not create the required joints.
Wide single easel back: generates a T-shaped support plus optional mating-slot geometry. A fixed slot connection is not the same as a hinge.
Narrow hinged rear strut: is one component of a picture-frame-style easel. It needs a front plaque, pivot hardware and a tether or stop.
Interlocking X-base: generates two half-slotted base bars only. The upright and plaque connection must be designed separately.

The purple coupon tests the chosen tab length and calculated slot width. Blue slot rectangles are mating geometry to position in the holder plate, not separate finished parts.

title: Laser-Cut Leg & Support Builder
text:
Before cutting

Measure the actual sheet thickness in several places.
Cut the fit coupon before the complete legs.
Open the SVG in Inkscape and confirm its physical dimensions at 100% scale.
Place matching slots in the holder plate and check that each slot has enough material around it.
Prototype in cardboard or scrap stock.
Assemble the real holder and test front-to-back and side-to-side tipping.

Use the Tool Organizer Project to plan and test the complete build. Use the Fabrication Plate Builder for the holder plate and repeated holes.

title: Laser-Cut Leg & Support Builder
section: Which reference file do I use?
text:
Which reference file do I use?
The SVG, DXF, DWG, CDR, PDF and PNG in the reference folder are different formats of the same template set. Do not combine all six files.

Use SVG in Inkscape. This is the easiest editable version for the laser workflow.
Use DXF or DWG in CAD/CAM software when that program handles those formats better.
Use CDR only in CorelDRAW.
Use PDF or PNG to look at or print the design. They are reference views, not the preferred editable cut file.

The external sheet contains several easel concepts. Select one complete matching group of parts, move that group into a new document, confirm the scale, and resize every slot for the measured sheet thickness. The reference was drawn around 0.118-inch material, which is slightly thinner than nominal 1/8-inch material. Always test one joint first.

title: Circuits
text:
Significant figures
Significant figures show the precision of a measured or stated value. Keep full calculator precision and round once, at the end.
0.00420 has three significant figures.
\(6.23 \times 1.23 = 7.6629\), reported as 7.66.
For multiplication and division, use the same number of significant figures as the least precise input. For addition and subtraction, use the least precise decimal place.

Scientific notation: \(a \times 10^n\), where \(1 \le a < 10\). Engineering notation: \(a \times 10^n\), where \(1 \le a < 1000\) and \(n\) is a multiple of three.
\(27\,000 = 2.7 \times 10^4 = 27 \times 10^3 = 27\,\mathrm{k}\) \(0.00047 = 4.7 \times 10^{-4} = 470 \times 10^{-6} = 470\,\mu\)

title: Circuits
text:
Ohm’s law and power
Ohm’s law connects voltage, current, and resistance.
\[
V = IR \qquad I = \frac{V}{R} \qquad R = \frac{V}{I}
\tag{1}\]
Equation Equation 1 gives the three general forms of Ohm’s law.
Electrical power is the rate of energy transfer:
\[
P = VI \qquad P = I^2R \qquad P = \frac{V^2}{R}
\tag{2}\]
Use Equation Equation 2 only after identifying the known quantities.
Use volts (V), amperes (A), ohms (\(\Omega\)), and watts (W). Convert prefixes before substituting, then report the final answer with the appropriate prefix and significant figures.

title: Circuits
text:
GUESS method
Put each part on its own line.
G: Given: list each known value with its symbol and unit.
U: Unknown: list each value you must find.
E: Equation: choose a general equation.
S: Substitute: rearrange first, then substitute values with units.
S: Solve: show the unrounded result, check it, then round once.
For a Casio calculator, enter one calculation per line. Use EXP for powers of ten. Write units beside the result, not in the calculator.

title: Circuits
text:
Circuit-analysis chapters
Use these notes with the matching teaching slides and question sheet.

Series circuits: one current path, voltage drops, resistance, and power.
Parallel circuits: common voltage, branch currents, equivalent resistance, and power.
Series-parallel circuits: identify groups, reduce, solve, expand, and check.
Kirchhoff’s laws: write current and voltage equations for networks that do not reduce directly.
Linear algebra for circuits: solve several node or loop equations together.

title: Linear Algebra for Circuits
Linear Algebra for Circuits
text:
Solve and check
Use substitution or elimination for a small system. Use a simultaneous-equation or matrix solver for a larger system. Keep the variable order and units consistent, then substitute the answer into the original equations or calculate the residual:
\[
\mathbf{r}=A\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{b}
\tag{4}\]
\[
\mathbf{r}\approx\mathbf{0}
\tag{5}\]
A large residual can flag a wrong sign, wrong measurement, or wiring fault.

text:
I will be able to identify a series circuit and calculate its total resistance, current, voltage drops, and power.
This is useful because I can predict every electrical value before building the circuit and check whether my measurements make sense.

title: Series Circuits
text:
I will be able to identify a series circuit and calculate its total resistance, current, voltage drops, and power.
This is useful because I can predict every electrical value before building the circuit and check whether my measurements make sense.
Used in college or university: Direct-current circuit analysis and circuit laboratories. [1, Ch. 4]
Where you see it: In a car, a lamp circuit can form one path through the battery, fuse, switch, and lamp. In a robot, a status light and current-limiting resistor form the same kind of path.

title: Series Circuits
text:
Series and parallel
A series circuit has one path, so the current is the same everywhere. A parallel circuit has branches that share the same two nodes, so each branch has the same voltage.



Figure 1. Series-circuit reference schematic. The same current passes through every component. #


Opening any component stops current everywhere.

title: Series Circuits
text:
General rules
\[
I_k = I_T
\tag{1}\]
\[
R_T = \sum_{k=1}^{n} R_k
\tag{2}\]
\[
V_T = \sum_{k=1}^{n} V_k
\tag{3}\]
\[
P_T = \sum_{k=1}^{n} P_k = V_T I_T
\tag{4}\]
\[
I_T = \frac{V_T}{R_T}
\tag{5}\]
\[
V_k = I_T R_k
\tag{6}\]
Here, \(k\) means any component in the path. Keep full calculator precision until the final answer.
\[
\sum_{k=1}^{n} V_k \overset{?}{=} V_T
\tag{7}\]
Use Equation Equation 7 to check the voltage drops. Also check power ratings.

title: Series Circuits
text:
Calculate then simulate
Calculate the circuit first. Build the same series and parallel circuits in Tinkercad, measure current and voltage, then compare the calculated and simulated values.

title: Engineering Preparation Track
text:
Engineering calculations
I will be able to use units, metric prefixes, engineering notation, significant figures, ratios, estimation, and the GUESS method.
This is useful because I can catch mistakes and communicate a calculation clearly.
Used in college or university: Every engineering course expects correct units, notation, and documented calculations. [1, Chs. 0–1]

title: Engineering Preparation Track
text:
Ohm’s law
I will be able to calculate voltage, current, and resistance and check whether the result is physically reasonable.
This is useful because I can predict the basic behaviour of a circuit before I build it.
Used in college or university: Circuit analysis, electronics laboratories, and design courses. [1, Chs. 1, 3]

title: Engineering Preparation Track
text:
Series circuits
I will be able to calculate total resistance, circuit current, and voltage drops in a one-path circuit.
This is useful because I can predict and check every value in a complete series circuit.
Used in college or university: Direct-current circuit analysis and introductory electrical laboratories. [1, Ch. 4]
Open the Series Circuits lesson package

title: Engineering Preparation Track
text:
Parallel circuits
I will be able to calculate equivalent resistance, source current, and branch currents in a parallel circuit.
This is useful because I can explain how several loads operate from the same source voltage.
Used in college or university: Network analysis, electrical distribution, instrumentation, and electronics. [1, Ch. 5]

title: Engineering Preparation Track
text:
Series-parallel circuits
I will be able to identify series and parallel groups, redraw a circuit, reduce it step by step, and work back to each branch value.
This is useful because I can turn a mixed circuit into smaller problems and prove the final answer.
Used in college or university: Network reduction, circuit laboratories, and preparation for Kirchhoff analysis. [1, Ch. 6]
Open the Series-Parallel Circuits lesson package

title: Engineering Preparation Track
text:
Kirchhoff’s laws
I will be able to apply Kirchhoff’s current law at a node and Kirchhoff’s voltage law around a loop.
This is useful because I can write equations for circuits that cannot be reduced by inspection.
Used in college or university: Nodal analysis, mesh analysis, electronics, power systems, and control hardware. [1, Ch. 9]






TipRecommended Grob sequence



Chapter 9 can follow Chapter 6. Students already have the series, parallel, and reduction skills needed for Kirchhoff analysis. Teach the relevant meter-safety material from Chapter 8 before physical measurements; Chapter 7 can be returned to later.

title: Engineering Preparation Track
text:
Linear algebra for circuits
I will be able to turn node and loop equations into a two- or three-variable system and solve it by elimination, substitution, matrices, and software.
This is useful because I can solve several unknown currents or voltages at the same time.
Used in college or university: Linear algebra, numerical methods, statics, structures, circuits, process models, and control. [28, Chs. 9, 12]

title: Engineering Preparation Track
text:
Work, energy, power, and efficiency
I will be able to distinguish work, energy, and power; use their derived units; and compare electrical energy input with useful mechanical work output.
This is useful because I can estimate battery use, motor performance, operating time, losses, and whether a device is doing useful work efficiently.
Planned laboratory: A small motor lifts a known mass through a measured height. Students measure motor voltage, current, and lift time, then compare the electrical energy supplied with the mechanical work completed and calculate input power, output power, and efficiency.
Used in college or university: Physics, mechanics, thermodynamics, circuits, electromechanical systems, and preparation for energy balances. [1, Chs. 3, 12, 14]

title: Engineering Preparation Track
text:
Equivalent circuits and optimization
I will be able to use dividers, Thévenin and Norton equivalents, maximum power transfer, constraints, and sensitivity.
This is useful because I can replace a complicated source network with a simpler model and compare designs.
Used in college or university: Circuit design, modelling, optimization, and instrumentation. [1, Chs. 7, 10]

title: Engineering Preparation Track
text:
Material and energy balances
I will be able to define a system boundary and calculate input, output, accumulation, loss, and efficiency.
This is useful because I can show where material or energy goes and explain what is lost.
Used in college or university: Chemical, mechanical, environmental, and energy engineering. [27, Chs. 3, 5–6]

title: Engineering Preparation Track
text:
Transient systems
I will be able to model resistor-capacitor charging, signal smoothing, and heating or cooling with time constants and numerical steps.
This is useful because I can predict how a real system changes over time instead of assuming it responds instantly.
Used in college or university: Differential equations, circuits, heat transfer, process dynamics, and control. [1, Ch. 22]

title: Engineering Preparation Track
section: Boolean logic, algorithms, and state machines
text:
Boolean logic, algorithms, and state machines
I will be able to interpret switches and digital sensor inputs as binary states and use logic gates, truth tables, Boolean expressions, algorithms, state diagrams, and test cases.
This is useful because I can turn physical on-or-off inputs into clear decisions that can be tested.
Used in college or university: Digital logic, programming, computer architecture, embedded systems, and control.

title: Engineering Preparation Track
text:
Number systems and digital representation
I will be able to use binary, decimal, hexadecimal, signed and unsigned integers, two’s complement, fixed-point, floating-point, analog-to-digital converter codes, pulse-width-modulation duty cycles, range, resolution, and overflow.
This is useful because I can explain how a computer stores a switch state, represents a sensor reading, and commands a variable output.
Used in college or university: Programming, computer engineering, embedded systems, numerical methods, and digital signal processing.

title: Engineering Preparation Track
text:
Sensors and measurement
I will be able to connect pull-up and pull-down switch inputs, read digital sensors, convert analog sensor signals with an analog-to-digital converter, use pulse-width modulation for controlled outputs, calibrate measurements, and report range, sensitivity, resolution, accuracy, repeatability, error, and uncertainty.
This is useful because I can move from a simple on-or-off input to a measured value and a controlled output while deciding whether the data is trustworthy.
Used in college or university: Engineering laboratories, instrumentation, embedded systems, robotics, experiments, and process control. [1, Ch. 8]

title: Engineering Preparation Track
text:
Motors and electromechanical systems
I will be able to calculate force, torque, speed, electrical input power, mechanical output power, efficiency, and operating limits.
This is useful because I can connect circuit behaviour and pulse-width-modulated control to useful motion.
Used in college or university: Mechanical, electrical, mechatronics, robotics, and systems engineering. [1, Chs. 13–14]

title: Engineering Preparation Track
text:
Sensor, logic, and actuator project
I will be able to combine digital or analog sensor inputs, thresholds, Boolean logic, pulse-width modulation, and a protected driver circuit to control a motor, fan, relay, alarm, or indicator.
This is useful because I can build a complete system that senses, decides, and acts safely.
Used in college or university: Mechatronics, embedded systems, robotics, automation, and design projects.

title: Engineering Preparation Track
section: Curve fitting, regression, and machine learning
text:
Curve fitting, regression, and machine learning
I will be able to fit a model to sensor data, inspect residuals, separate training and test data, and compare prediction error with a baseline.
This is useful because I can find a useful pattern without assuming the first model is correct.
Used in college or university: Data analysis, numerical methods, system identification, experiments, and introductory machine learning. [28, Chs. 17, 20]

title: Engineering Preparation Track
text:
Operational amplifiers and calculus
I will be able to analyze ideal operational-amplifier circuits and connect integrator and differentiator circuits to slope, area, and rate of change.
This is useful because I can see calculus operate on a real voltage signal.
Used in college or university: Calculus, analog electronics, instrumentation, signals, and control. [1, Ch. 33]

title: Engineering Preparation Track
text:
Feedback and control
I will be able to compare open-loop, on-off, hysteresis, proportional, integral, and derivative control using response, error, stability, and saturation.
This is useful because I can make a system correct itself and explain why poor settings cause problems.
Used in college or university: Control systems, robotics, mechatronics, chemical processes, and automation.

title: Engineering Preparation Track
text:
Engineering design project
I will be able to define requirements, model a system, create a schematic and program, select sensors and actuators, build or simulate, test, validate, and revise.
This is useful because I can combine the track into one working, evidence-based design.
Used in college or university: Design courses, laboratories, capstone projects, and technical communication.

title: Engineering Preparation Track
text:
Ontario course collaboration opportunities
These are places where teachers can plan shared investigations or projects. They do not mean that one course replaces the learning in another course.

Computer engineering technology
Courses: TEJ3M and TEJ4M
Shared work: Circuit calculations, schematics, simulation, construction, measurement, troubleshooting, sensors, motors, digital logic, data representation, and pulse-width modulation.
Good collaboration: TEJ students can design, build, program, and troubleshoot the measurement or control system used by another class. This connects directly to TEJ3M A3.1–A3.3, B3.1–B3.4, and B5.3, and TEJ4M A3.2–A3.5, A5.2–A5.6, and B3.1–B3.4. Ontario Technological Education curriculum


Physics
Course: SPH3U
Shared work: Charge, voltage, current, resistance, power, energy, series circuits, parallel circuits, mixed circuits, Ohm’s law, Kirchhoff’s laws, meters, motors, and generators.
Good collaboration: Use the same circuit problem set and laboratory data in both courses. Physics can emphasize the model and equations; TEJ can emphasize the schematic, safe construction, measurement, and troubleshooting. This supports SPH3U F2.1–F2.3, F2.6, F2.8, and F3.3–F3.9. SPH3U expectations


Chemistry
Course: SCH4U
Shared work: Electrochemical cells, batteries, cell potential, current, energy, efficiency, data collection, graphing, uncertainty, and significant figures.
Good collaboration: Chemistry students can build a galvanic cell and explain the redox reactions while TEJ students measure its open-circuit voltage, loaded voltage, current, power, and internal resistance. This connects especially to SCH4U F2.4–F2.5 and the A1 scientific-investigation skills. SCH4U expectations


Biology
Course: SBI4U
Shared work: Sensors, calibration, data logging, graphs, uncertainty, stimulus-response investigations, and feedback systems.
Good collaboration: TEJ students can build and validate a light, temperature, moisture, heart-rate, or respiration data logger. Biology students then use it to investigate a biological question and interpret the evidence. This connects naturally to SBI4U A1 and E2.2–E2.4; the electronics are the instrument, not a substitute for the biology. SBI4U expectations


Shared science practices
All three science partnerships can use the same habits taught at the start of this track: choose suitable instruments, control variables, record data in tables and graphs, analyse error and uncertainty, use SI units, and report calculations with appropriate significant figures.

title: Choosing a Linux Distribution
text:
A Linux distribution, or distro, is a complete operating system built around Linux. Distros are a little like different flavours: they share many ingredients, but each has its own installer, desktop, software choices, update system, and community. No flavour is best for everyone, although people often have strong preferences. Some distributions are also based on other distributions.
For example:
Debian
└── Ubuntu
    ├── Linux Mint
    └── Lubuntu
Debian is a long-running, community-built distribution known for stability. Ubuntu is based on Debian and aims to make Linux practical for a wide range of users. The African word ubuntu is often translated as “I am because we are.” Linux Mint is a child of Ubuntu: it uses Ubuntu as a foundation and adds its own desktop experience and tools.

title: Choosing a Linux Distribution
text:
Our choice: Linux Mint Xfce
We will use Linux Mint 22.3 “Zena” Xfce Edition because it works well and is easy for students to begin using. Xfce is the desktop interface. Its layout feels a little like older versions of Windows, and it runs quickly on our older computers with less than 8 GB of RAM. It starts simple, but we can improve and personalize the way it looks later.
Lubuntu is another good lightweight flavour to explore. If you want to compare many possibilities, try the questions at Distrochooser.

title: Choosing a Linux Distribution
section: Release styles: a stable base or the newest software
text:
Release styles: a stable base or the newest software
Ubuntu publishes a new version every six months, usually in April and October. Its version number shows the year and month: 24.04 means April 2024. Releases also have names, such as Ubuntu 24.04 “Noble Numbat.”
Every two years, the April release is an LTS, or Long Term Support, release. LTS versions receive updates for much longer than the releases between them, making them a dependable base for a classroom or everyday computer. Linux Mint 22.3 “Zena” uses the Ubuntu 24.04 LTS package base and is supported until April 2029. We can keep an LTS-based system for work and experiment with a faster-moving distribution on another computer, in a virtual machine, or later as part of a dual-boot setup.
Arch uses a rolling-release model instead of publishing separate LTS versions on a fixed timetable. You install it once and update it continuously, so new software arrives quickly. This gives you current software and a great deal of control, but it also asks you to read update notices, make decisions, and troubleshoot more often.
Arch Linux is the most difficult option discussed here. It expects you to assemble and configure much more of the system yourself. That makes it a poor first classroom installation, but a valuable future challenge if you want to become a system administrator and understand or control every part of a Linux system.
In my classes, students who chose Arch and persisted through its difficulties have often gone on to considerable success in computer engineering, including major scholarship and job opportunities. Arch itself is not a shortcut to those outcomes. The persistence, research, troubleshooting, and systems thinking required to make it work are excellent preparation.
For this lab, our choice is Linux Mint Xfce. In a future lab, we will choose another operating system and install it alongside Windows to create a dual-boot computer.

title: Install Linux Mint 22.3 Xfce
text:
Linux Mint is a Linux operating system that usually just works and is easy for new users. We are installing Linux Mint 22.3 “Zena” Xfce Edition. Xfce has a familiar, classic Windows-like layout and uses fewer system resources, which makes it a good fit for our older computers with less than 8 GB of RAM.
This classroom guide is adapted from the official Linux Mint Installation Guide. The installer screenshots come from that guide. Screens can change slightly between releases, and the example names or checkboxes shown in a screenshot may not match our required classroom settings. Follow the written choices on this page.

title: Install Linux Mint 22.3 Xfce
text:
Before you begin
You need:

the assigned classroom computer;
a Linux Mint 22.3 “Zena” Xfce USB installer signed out from your teacher;
the classroom Wi-Fi credentials; and
your lab log.

Disconnect any personal USB drives or external storage. Have the teacher confirm the target computer before you erase anything.

How the classroom USB was made
The teacher, with help from student volunteers, prepared the bootable USB drives before this lab. They downloaded the Linux Mint Xfce .iso image from the official Linux Mint download page and used balenaEtcher to write the image to a USB drive. On Windows, Rufus is another good tool for creating a bootable USB.
An ISO cannot simply be copied onto a USB like an ordinary file. A tool such as Etcher or Rufus writes the image in a form the computer can start from. This process erases the USB drive, so do not try it with a personal drive unless its contents are safely backed up.
For this lab, sign out a prepared USB from your teacher. Record its number if your class uses numbered drives, and return it when the installation is complete.

title: Install Linux Mint 22.3 Xfce
text:
1. Start the live system
Insert the Linux Mint USB drive, then start or restart the computer. You need to choose the USB as the startup device before the existing operating system loads.

On the classroom Intel iMacs and Mac minis

Press the power button or restart the Mac.
Immediately hold Option (⌥) or Alt until Startup Manager appears.
Select the USB drive (it may appear as EFI Boot) and press Enter/Return. If the USB does not appear, stop and ask your teacher.

Apple documents the Option/Alt startup shortcut in its Intel Mac startup-key guide.


On a Windows PC
The startup key is different for almost every manufacturer and model. Common keys include Delete, F1, F2, F10, F11, F12, and Escape.

Watch the first manufacturer-logo screen for a message such as Boot Menu, Boot Options, Setup, BIOS, or UEFI.
Press the listed key repeatedly as the computer starts. Try the one-time Boot Menu first and select the USB drive.
If there is no boot menu, enter the BIOS/UEFI settings and, with teacher approval, temporarily move the USB drive ahead of the internal drive in the boot order. Do not change unrelated settings.

If the key is not shown, search for manufacturer model boot menu key or manufacturer model boot from USB. Include the exact manufacturer and model printed on the computer. The official Linux Mint boot guide also lists common keys.
Choose the normal Start Linux Mint option when the Linux Mint startup menu appears. Linux Mint first opens a live session: a temporary desktop running from the USB drive.
The live session may feel slower than the finished installation, and changes made there are not permanent. If the live session asks for a password, leave it blank and press Enter.
Double-click Install Linux Mint on the desktop.

title: Install Linux Mint 22.3 Xfce
text:
5. Choose the installation type
Select Erase disk and install Linux Mint.

Leave Advanced features at its default setting with None selected. We can explore advanced storage settings in a later lab.
Do not select an encryption option for this classroom installation.
Do not select Something else.
Do not select an “install alongside” option in this lab.




Linux Mint installation-type screen with Erase disk and install Linux Mint selected.


Select Install Now or Continue, depending on the wording shown. Read the drive-change summary, confirm that it refers to the approved classroom drive, and then continue.
In a future lab, we will install another operating system alongside Windows and create a dual-boot computer. That is not today’s task.






WarningDual-boot installations use different instructions



If you are installing Linux on your own computer and want to keep Windows, stop here and do not choose “Erase disk and install Linux Mint.” A dual-boot installation requires a current backup, enough free storage, and a careful plan for the computer’s partitions, encryption, firmware, and recovery options.
It is usually easier to install Windows first and Linux second. Windows installation can replace the existing boot sequence, while Linux Mint normally detects Windows and creates a menu for choosing an operating system at startup. See Linux Mint’s official multi-boot guidance.
Before changing partitions, check whether Windows uses BitLocker/device encryption, save its recovery key, and research the exact computer model. An encrypted Windows drive may prevent a Linux installer from safely examining or resizing the Windows partitions. Ubuntu’s BitLocker dual-boot explanation describes this issue clearly.
Some computers have two internal SSDs. Installing each operating system on a separate drive can make the layout easier to understand and can reduce the chance of accidentally changing the other system’s partitions or boot files. However, this is not a rule of EFI/UEFI, and it is not required on every computer. Firmware behaviour varies, even between Lenovo Legion models, so search the manufacturer, exact model, and terms such as dual boot, UEFI, and boot order before proceeding. Use a model-specific guide and ask for experienced help rather than guessing.
